It is asserted by the press of this country that the Conservative party in this House are wasting the time of the House, are delaying the business of parliament, are incurring unduly large expense by continuing the debate on this Address; in fact, by way of excuse, some -of them have pretended to find some justification for us in alleging that under the rules of the House the Address must take precedence and that it is impossible to conduct any other business in the House while the Address is under debate. I wish to state clearly that there are no such rules. The position in which we are placed 4 p.m. is due to the specific resolutions moved by the hon. leader of the House (Mr. Lapointe) and adopted by this House, some of them under our protest and on division.
Fir^t, the acting leader of the government moved a resolution on a certain day that the debate on the Address have precedence over .all other public and private business in this .House, and then, having obtained the passage

Instead of saying that mentally and intellectually my hon. friend is afflicted with Brights disease, I will recall the statement and say that it is the Cdbden-Bright disease, which I think entirely obscures his mental vision and prevents him from studying the real interests of the country as a whole. I remember, Mr. Speaker, many years ago swinging on a gate in front of my father's home and seeing the carriages with their flags go by, carrying the voters to the first election held in Canada after the union of 1867. Since that time I may say that Canada has held my supreme affection, and whatever oourse I may have taken, whatever mistakes I may have made, there was always in my heart a desire to see a Canadian nationality established politically independent of the United States of America, and maintaining its due relationship to England and to the sister colonies. In order to build up Canada on those lines, my old province of Nova Scotia, which has ever been associated by respect and esteem- I might almost say affection-with the other Maritime provinces and the province of Quebec, has united with the provinces in the east to carry forward policies which were not necessarily of great advantage to themselves, but were of public interest and necessary for the development of Canada as a whole. If we had been wanting in that spirit of patriotism; if we had been wanting in the spirit of selfsacrifice; and if we had not in the eastern province developed our commercial and industrial institutions to a considerable degree, Canada's international credit would never have been sufficient to enable her to raise the funds necessary to carry through the first line of railway into the northwest and to open up that country for our settlers. Had it not been for that spirit, Saskatchewan to-day would be growing prairie grass and over-run by buffalo, as it was in my boyhood days. But I do not wish to recount these things. We built those roads in the early days out of a spirit of Canadian patriotism; we made sacrifices for the good of the whole country in the building up and development of the northwest. With that spirit-and I am well acquainted with the people from the Maritime provinces-I do not believe there is in

The Address-Mr. Cahan
this House a member from any of those districts who will cavil at any measure which is brought forward and which is necessary for the proper development of the northwest and the general prosperity and wellbeing of the people of those western districts.
One hon. member, I think he was a member of the Liberal party, delivered an address at some length in which he spoke of agriculture as being one of the primary industries of this country and referred to the absolute necessity of encouraging the farming industry, especially the interests of the wheat growers of the west. In that I entirely agree with him. But the people otf Canada cannot live by wheat alone; they require other industries than that of raising wheat. I remember in my province, when the middle west was opened1 up and produced wheat at a lower figure than that at which we could raise it, our farmers were driven out of that branch of farming known as the production of wheat. I remember being told in my early days that the old Grand Pre valley, which is now used for ordinary farming, was one of the best wheat producing districts in the world1 as to quality, having due regard to the size and extent of the area planted. But those days are gone, and it is necessary that members of this Hotae should have a broad perspective in dealing with questions relating to ithe future of this country. I know something about wheat growing, and I will venture to say 'that I have a farm with a wheat field which will compare favourably with any two wheat fields owned by any two members of the Progressive or Liberal party from Alberta or Saskatchewan. I know something about the wheat trade, and I say to them that in a branch of farming which is largely speculative under present conditions they have reached the heydiay of their prosperity if they continue to grow wheat alone When you find Russia on its feet again and producing wheat; when you have more competition-and it is bound to come-from Australia and Argentina, you farmers of the west will discover that unless you can grow wheat and put it on the market at your own railway stations at something like seventy or seventy-five cents a bushel, you will be forced into other forms of production in order to maintain the prosperity of those provinces. But in the meantime I concede that that industry, which was encouraged especially during the war and which gave not only to us but to the armies of the allies their sustenance through that great conflict, will never make any reasonable appeal to the whole body of this House without receiving a unanimous response.
We are all as anxious to benefit Saskatchewan as we are to further the interests of any other province. But when the hon. member for Rosetown rises in his place and speaks of the poverty of the farmers of that province, I wish to tell 'him that according to statistics compiled by the government of this country, no other province in Canada has as great wealth per capita as Saskatchewan. The western provinces come first in per capita wealth, Saskatchewan holding the first place with a per capita wealth of $3,757, Alberta second with a per 'capita wealth of $3,317, and Manitoba third with a per capita wealth of $2,705, as compared with Ontario, $2,507, and Quebec, $2,347, while Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have one-half the per capita wealth of Saskatchewan. I say to theim that in every matter we of the east have dealt or endeavoured to deal with them fairly. When they were carved out as provinces from the territories of the west, parliament was unanimous in giving them large subsidies from the federal treasury in order that they might be placed' in a really excellent position to carry out their work in building up new provinces from those territories. But Nova Scotia, if we take it as it is to-day with a population of 523,837, receives from the federal government by the way of subsidy $661,853, while Saskatchewan, with a somewhat higher population-828,600-received more than three times as much, namely, $1,757,005 per annum. That is, Saskatchewan, with 58 per cent more population than Nova Scotia, receives 165 per cent more subsidy from the federal treasury of this country. We of the east look upon this country as a whole. We cannot live by bread alone. The development of natural resources such as coal, the fisheries and the lumber from our forests is on an equal basis with the development of agriculture.

Just for information, I
would like to ask the hon. member if he knows 'how those per capita figures are made up in regard to the wealth of the people of the different provinces. Do they take into consideration liabilities by way of mortgages or other indebtedness of individuals in the several provinces?

I am reading from one of
the reports issued by the Bureau of Statistics, published under the authority of Hon. T. A. Low, MJ?., 1924, at Ottawa, entitled, A Report on the National Wealth of Canada and its Provinces. I am accepting that as a fair criterion in a general way of the position as regards the wealth of the different provinces. The government of this country,
The Address-Mr. Cahan

through its Bureau of Statistics, has entered upon an inquiry as to the productive activities upon which the prosperity of Canada depends, and it proceeds on the basis that such productive activities may be ascertained from year to year by consideration of the net value of commodities produced in this country for consumption at home and for export abroad. Making this computation on a broad basis, the Bureau of Statistics estimates approximately the national income of the Canadian people and thereby ascertains the values available for the maintenance of our own citizens, for the support of all public services, for taxation of every sort, and for the annual accretions of savings for the increase in future of these industrial activities. They take the year 1923, the very latest for which they have complete statistics, showing that in that year agriculture yielded
81.107.000.	000 of produce. Economists both in this country and in the United States have criticized that figure as an over-estimate due to the fact that a considerable portion of the products of agriculture was used on the farm for seeding purposes and for the maintenance of farm animals and the like. They declare that that 81,107,000,000, in relation to the further figures which I am about to quote, should be somewhat reduced.
Of forestry, fisheries, trapping, mining and the development of electrical power, hydroelectric largely, the net income of the Canadian people was $854,0001,000. Thus the value created by the industry of this country, comprising manufacturing;, construction and repairs, exceeds by more than half as much again the value produced by the entire agricultural industry of this whole country.
I am quite walling to admit that of that agricultural production practically one-third in 1923 was wheat alone, and therefore I have always contended that Wheat production must receive peculiarly favourable consideration from the people of this country. But the manufacturing industry of Canada created

The hon. member will

Quite so; and there is not

For example a certain quantity of the wool of this country or of cotton imported from -abroad is subjected to various processes of manufacture, all of which involve the use of machinery of some kind, and these processes contribute to the creation of wealth, which forms a part of the tangible income of the country. Now, in creating a billion and a half of manufactured wealth in 1923 we gave employment in Canada to a large body of our people in cities, towns and villages; and if that manufacturing industry is imperilled, as it was imperilled by the pronouncements of this government a year ago, I am prepared to -prove that there will be driven from this country into foreign countries 45 per cent of our existing population, who will go elsewhere to -produce the same things that they are producing in Canada to-day. Therefore the man who works in a factory and helps in that way to create wealth is doing as essential a work and is discharging as patriotic a duty as are the 250,000 farmers of the west and of Canada who are producing wheat, which sails overseas and is sold at such prices as the impoverished people of middle Europe can afford to pay for the temporary sustenance which 'they require in order to carry on the industries of those countries. Well, if the hon. gentleman

The policy which I advocate is the policy which the Premier of Quebec and his associates have been advocating for some years. They have laid down the sound economic doctrine that no country grows wealthy, no peoples become prosperous, simply by producing raw materials for export, simply by becoming hewers of wood and drawers of water for foreign peoples. My hon. friend will have noticed that the hon. Mr. Caron- I think he is the Minister of Agriculture in the provincial government of Quebec-has been making address after address throughout his province in which he has declared that it is absolutely necessary for its well-being that there should be protection of farm products. I refer particularly to Mr. Caron's letter to the secretar5' of the Societe Agricole of St. Cesaire of March 5, 1925, in which, if I recollect
correctly, he laid down the policy of protection for the farm products of that province. The government of Quebec, almost alone of our provincial governments, has prohibited, so far as it could under the constitution, the export of pulpwood to the United States, insisting that all the pulpwood taken off the crown lands of that province should be manufactured within its borders in order to give increased employment and increased prosperity to its people. That government has also during the present session of the legislature introduced a bill prohibiting the export of hydro-electric power to any foreign country. It has proposed and, according to the statements of the premier, is now considering measures for restraining to a certain extent tbo export of asbestos in order to encourage its manufacture in the province. In short, within its constitutional powers the government of Quebec is carrying out in every way possible a policy of protection for home industries and of encouraging other industries to come into the province. I do not intend to discuss with any member from the province the question of protection in Quebec.

I know something about that province, and I think I can say without fear of contradiction that in its principal towns there is a strong feeling in favour of a protective tariff to the extent necessary to safeguard domestic industries. In some of the rural districts where the people realize that their best market, in fact in some cases their only market, is in the neighbouring towns and villages, there has been a growing feeling in favour of safeguarding and protecting the farm products of Quebec; and any person who imagines he can appeal to the provinces on the sole issue of free trade is mightily mistaken if he thinks he can obtain there any general support for such a policy.
To pursue my general argument, we have in the last five years-and I am referring to it

Those people have been driven abroad by what I regard as the entirely mistaken policy of the government of the day. I remember very well the unpleasant thrill which went through industrial circles in eastern Canada in March, 1923, when the legislature of Saskatchewan-under the leadership of the Hon. Mr. Dunning, who, I understand, has become the chief counsellor of the Prime Minister and is slated to become a member of this government-on March 1, 1923, unanimously passed this resolution:
Resolved, that in the opinion of this assembly, it is the duty of the government of Canada to introduce legislation which shaill 'have for its effect the following:
(1)	An immediate and substantial all-round reduction of the customs tariff.
(2)	The reduction of the customs duty on goods imported from Great Britain to one-half of the rates charged under the general tariff, and that further gradual uniform reductions be made to the remaining tariff on British imports that will insure complete free trade between Great Britain and Canada.
The economic and tariff policies proclaimed by Mr. Dunning in Saskatchewan and unanimously endorsed by the legislature of Saskatchewan, were taken up in the following year and led to certain enunciations of policy from the Prime Minister of this country from his seat in the House on May 15, 1924. In his address on the budget in the House of Commons Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King announced his policy as follows:
No more tariffs based on the principle of protection -as set forth in the resolution of the Tory party, moved in this debate too late to be accepted-but a tariff based on the -principle of revenue. That was "our policy" in the. past-the Laurier-Fielding policy. The words can have no other meaning. That is our policy to-day-the policy of the Liberal party-proceeding step by step towards the goal of greater freedom in matters of trade, never imposing a duty for protection's sake, but ail ways acting on the principle or the basis of a tariff for revenue and revenue only. I repeat this statement in the hearing of -hon. members and before this country, this is the position of the Liberal party. We believe in proceeding step by step. We believe when it comes to a question of imposing a duty in having duties framed on a tariff for revenue basis and not on a basis of protection.

But when that statement was made to this country, with the further decreases which were made by the British preferential tariff, it led to great anxiety on the part of every man who was engaged in industrial enterprises in Canada. It stopped entirely the investment of new capital in almost every industry in this country. It prevented the establishment of new industries which were about to be established in the Dominion. There was ample money available in the country, and yet that money instead of seeking employment in industrial enterprises became a supply to compete for certain stocks which were regarded as likely to stand the strain of a revenue tariff pure and simple. We had a great increase in the value of bank stocks, and there was greater competition for their purchase. There was great competition in this country for the purchase of American standard stocks, and more than that: millions of dollars of Canadian capital were transferred month by month to the United States seeking employment in the industrial affairs of that country, where a safe and sound economic policy was in operation and where there was less doubt as to the stability of those enterprises under the conditions which prevailed there. Factory after factory to my knowledge, if it is necessary to go into it, which were employing men and women in the province of Quebec-ordinary industrial enterprises quite proper and suitable to our climate and our conditions, -giving employment to thousands of people, were transformed not into manufacturing establishments but into depots to which millions of dollars' worth of manufactured goods were brought from France, England, Italy, Belgium and Germany, and thence distributed to the people of this country. Thousands of people lost their industrial employment in consequence. The Right Hon.

The Address-Mr. Cahan
Mackenzie King, in announcing that policy, was directly responsible for sending a very considerable number of our young men across the border to seek employment. In the city of Montreal there is destitution to-day the like of which we did not know when we had a stable tariff and stable conditions in our industrial life. There people are out of employment by the hundreds; women and children are under-nurtured; those who were born and brought up in fairly comfortable circumstances and became expert workmen are too poor to-day to sustain the life of their children but too proud to beg, and a generation of children are growing up undernurtured-all simply because the Right Hon. Mackenzie King attempted to put into operation, so far as he could, a tariff policy that opened up our industries to the unfair competition of foreign countries. And not only that; he declared his intention to put such a tariff into force completely, thus threatening to drive our people out of employment and to force out of this country at least 45 per cent of its present population.
Mr. Speaker, I have made a careful analysis of the imports into this country, amounting to about $850,000,000 or $900,000,000 a year, and I am prepared at an opportune time to show that at least $500,000,000 of those annual imports might, under a proper tariff policy, under a proper economic policy, be produced by the people of Canada, giving direct employment to at least 350,000 or
500,000	more employees that at present have work in this Dominion, and sustaining an additional 1,000,000 to 1,250,000 people.	I
listened the other day with the greatest possible interest to the splendid address of the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Tolmie) on the question of immigration, and I quite approve of every pronouncement which he made, as I understand it. But it is not sufficient to bring in 250,000 men to go on the farms of the west or even to settle on the farms of the east if we have under proper conditions a proper tariff policy-I do not say a high tariff or a low tariff.
I agree entirely with the pronouncement made the other day by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) that what we need in this country is a safeguarding tariff that will give fair play and fair operation to the industries of this country, and protect them from the competition of certain countries with a debased currency, from the cheaper labour of Europe and from the mass production of the United States. We need a tariff that will enable us to build up here, as they have done in the United States, a great and growing industrial community which 14011-70
will give employment to our own sons and daughters for generations to come and so increase our employment that we may invite into this country not only farmers to come and till the land, but expert artisans of other countries who will teach us to carry on an improved industrial life in certain particulars, and enable us to establish factories for the production of many other articles either of necessity or of luxury which we now import from foreign countries.
That a growing export trade is sure indi-' cation of increasing wealth, well-being and prosperity on the part of the people is often stated in this House and throughout the country. A more damnable heresy never was preached. Take the country os you find it. For instance, I called your attention the other night to a country like Mexico, and I deal with it because I know from personal experience its conditions. Mexico is gifted by providence with natural resources unequalled by those of any other country I know of. Glance at what they might do, with a population larger than ours-some fourteen or fifteen millions of people.
Mexico has more sugar cane land than Cuba; more citrous fruit land than the United States and Italy combined; more tobacco land than the West Indies; more cocoanut land than the Philippine Islands; more banana land than central America; more corn land than any other country in the world except the United States. It produces more coffee than any country in the world outside of Brazil; cotton is grown in many parts of it. Mexico is the greatest producer of silver in the world; it ranks next to the United States in the production of copper; it produces large quantities of lead; it has the largest sulphate deposits in the world, as well as valuable tin beds and coal fields in the north; as an oil producer it is second to the United States. Yet with all these resources, year after year the peon and the Indian of Mexico toil for 50 cents of our money a day to develop these natural resources and send the products out of the country where they are employed as raw materials and oil for motive power in carrying on the industries of other countries. The natural resources of Mexico form the basis of industries which are carried on in the United States, in Great Britain, in Belgium and in France. A country with the most marvellous natural resources in the world giving itself up to the damnable policy of exporting its natural resources to other countries, leaving its people at home the most impoverished on the face of the north or south American continent! That is the condition which the tariff policy of the Right

It is due to the fact that they have not any. I remember very well in my own province of Nova Scotia

and I knew it well from almost end to end-our village life and our town life waS sustained by small industries employing five, ten, fifteen or twenty people. Look at the conditions in any industrialized country.

The Address-Mr. Cahan
The name of Jules Maline will ever be revered throughout the Republic of France, because he gave to the farmers of that country a protective tariff which established on a firm foundation the financial stability of the republic and enabled it to stand, as it did, all the horrors of invasion and war. I know some of the professors at Laval. Some of them have been brought from foreign countries; others are native-born, and they are equal to any of those who do similar work in the United States. In McGill University we are training and spending thousands of dollars upon the education of our young people, yet by the tariff policies of the country we are precluding the establishment and operation of industries which might give them employment under stable conditions. We are sending thousands of highly and technically educated young men out of the country year by year to seek employment. A policy such as that is most detrimental to our future progress, and unless we provide a remedy we never can reach a high state of national development.

I desire to say a word to my Progressive friends; I observe that some of them have disappeared under my eloquence. One of them statqd last night that prices should be fixed so as to give to the farmers a fairly remunerative return for their industry, including not merely a reasonable interest upon their capital, but remunerative employment for themselves and a living for their families. With that statement I entirely agree. If we are to build up and co-ordinate our industrial structure, that must be one of the elements of it. The farmer is entitled to exactly the same consideration that we give or will give to the manufacturing industries of the country. He is entitled to no more and should receive no less.
Referring to another feature of the present conditions in the country which preclude development-taxation and the public debt- I may point out that we incurred a public debt of $1,600,000,000 in round figures, during the war and the three years and a half of demobilization following the war. That is an enormous debt, and it weighs as a heavy burden upon the people. But during the last eight years, a period equal to that covered by the period of the war and the years of demobilization, the public obligations of this country have been increased by over $800,000,000 in connection with the Canadian National Railways. That is, in the last eight years, heaped up upon the burden of debt created by the war, we have created new obligations equal to one-half the same amount which we are now shouldering for the purpose of carrying on those railways under the conditions under which they are carried on. That is a problem which is giving great anxiety to every man who has at heart the best interests of this country, a problem which the govern-
The Address-Mr. Cahan

ment must solve, a problem which, as I will attempt to show in a few moments, it undertook to solve before making its appeal to the country in the last general election.
Our taxation weighs upon our people today as a grievous burden. Twenty-live per cent of the entire productive income of this country goes year by year to pay the federal, provincial and municipal taxes which are imposed upon our people. On the average, every Canadian workman, out of a year of twelve months, if he works twelve months stead%, gives approximately three months of his toil to earn sufficient to pay the taxes which are placed upon him. That burden is too great, and it must be reduced if we are to maintain the industrial activities of this country and to keep our people in Canada. I find that the United States of America reduced their annual federal expenditures from
85,538,000,060 in 1920-21 to 83,619,000,000 in 1925-26, a reduction of 81,919,000,000, or one-third of their entire annual expenditure in that period. During the same period they reduced their federal debt by 84,000,000,000 and their annual interest charges by 8179,000,000. One-sixth of their public debt was wiped out. There has been a reduction in the cost of public services and an increase in domestic employment. Remunerative employment has been given to five million more people, thereby increasing the consumption of agricultural products in the United States during that period by eighteen per cent if we reckon in quantity and not in price. The cost of the executive services handled from Washington was reduced by 81,364,000,000 a year and the federal payroll was 115,000 employees less on December 31, 1925, than it was *on the same date five years previously. During the past year the staffs at Washington were reduced by five thousand; employees, and in the federal civil; administration alone, which is the same as our civil list or our civil service at Ottawa, the sum of 860,000,000 was saved in twelve months. Such reductions as these in the United States mean large reductions in taxation, decreases in the annual fiscal burden of the whole body of the people, an increased purchasing power for every person domiciled in that country, a higher standard of living owing to the increased purchasing power, and an increased industrial saving throughout that nation giving them larger capital for investment in other enterprises. This is what President Coolidge said about a year ago in reviewing these facts:
Past experience has shown that a reduction of taxes has been followed by increased prosperity. As the volume of business increases, the federal revenue increases. If we are moderate in our expenditures the 
natural increase in profits ought, within a few years, to furnish us still with a surplus revenue, which will permit further tax reduction.
This country is demanding to-day, not only that there shall be a decrease in the annual cost o,f government, federal, provincial and municipal, but that those expenditures shall be cut down right to the bone, until it hurts, because under present conditions applicable not only to federal, but to provincial and municipal affairs, we are lowering the standard of living in this country by one-fourth owing to taxation. We are taking . one-fourth of the wages of every man woman and child in this country for the purposes of taxation, and the people of Canada demand that sincere, honest and effective effort be made to reduce those expenditures to the lowest possible limit.
Such was the condition of affairs when the leader of the government made his appeal to the country in September last. We had then and had had for years an increasing lack of remunerative employment in this country. We had had increasing taxation under which the people were groaning and we had a railway condition which demanded earnest, careful attention. We had a preferential treatment of Great Britain and certain foreign countries, not only under the preferential tariff jbut under treaties, enabling producers in foreign countries to send into Canada their manufactured commodities and thus drive our people out of employment and as far as possible out of the country. The Right Hon. Mackenzie King decided upon an appeal to the people to place these issues and his proposed solution of them before the electorate of the whole country for their final decision. He first interviewed His Excellency the Governor General, stating to him the grounds on which he intended to make that appeal, and fortunately we have an official report made by himself of the grounds which he presented to His Excellency the Governor General and on which he demanded1 the right of dissolution of parliament and of appealing. On September 6, 1925, when speaking at Richmond Hill at the opening of the campaign, and announcing for the first time the date of the approaching general election, the right hon. gentleman said, according to the Canadian Press report, which on inquiry I find was handed by his own secretary to the press, previously written out:
The Prime Minister said that the government could have heUd on to office for many months yet and still have been within the limits of the constitution, in fact until February, 1927. But he stated that the ministry of which he is the head, had come to the conclusion that for an administration to give the best service to Canada at this important time, it should

The Address-Mr. Cahan
have a fresh mandate from the ejectors on several questions, the disposal of which will vitally affect the future of 'this country. His government, he asserted, had never been impelled by purely political motives in any of its acts since it was formed, and now, although it could have continued in office without an election, and perhaps continued to receive the substantial majorities it had enjoyed in the past, it had decided in the interests of Canada that the people should pronounce on the issues on which his party would appeal. There were four issues he said which over-shadowed all others: first, the fiscal policy; second, the railway problem; third, the immigration problem; and fourth, the reform of the Senate.
After discussing the right of the government of which he was Prime Minister to request from His Excellency the Governor General a dissolution of parliament, the right hon. gentleman said:
Next to be considered is the question of the ability of the government to carry on. So far as the House of Commons is concerned, I see no reason to believe that such support as we have all along been able to command in parliament will not continue to be accorded the administration another session. So far as the country is concerned, I believe we possess its confidence to-day to a degree greater than at any time since we came into office. Can there be any doubt that the federal administration has steadily grown in public confidence?
The Prime Minister then considered, from his own and his party's point of view, the following views which had been presented to him with respect to the advisability of holding an election at that time,-the existing commercial and industrial depression, which he recognized, and the prospect which he said existed of an early revival of trade and industry. He then continued:
If we arc to look at public questions solely from the point of view of party political advantage, this argument and some of the others I have mentioned might appear to have much more force. For a government that has in its favour all the factors I have enumerated, not to speak of numerous other considerations, deliberately -to forego more than a year of the time for which it has the right to continue in office, is a step which, in the eyes of the public, to say nothing of the eyes of its own following, requires not a little by way of justification. Indeed, under existing circumstances, the responsibility of advising a dissolution of parliament would appear to be quite as great as that of continuing to carry on, despite all the difficulties of government which we necessarily experience.
Are immediate party considerations, may I ask, the only ones that are to govern, or chiefly to govern, in the management of a nation's affairs? I can say of the present administration, since its assumption of office, that purely party considerations have never been permitted to override the national interests, nor wiiil they now be a determining factor in reaching a decision on a matter of first national importance. Party is most important, but at must be remembered that party is the instrument, not the end, of government. Each is essential to the other; without a party, and a strong party at that, very little in the way of good government can be effected. The end of government is the well-being of the country, the happiness, the prosperity and the contentment of its
people. Party is the means to that end, the means of uniting in a common aim and effort men and women who feel and think alike on the problems of government, the instrumetit for bringing about the policies which it is desired to make prevail. The best party strategy has in view always what in the long run is for the best of the country.
I commend these sentiments to the acting leader of the government (Mr. Lapointe) and those associated with him just now in carrying on this government in the dilapidated condition in which we find it. Further, the Prime Minister said:
That brings me to the situation with which at the moment the government is faced. As a government we can carry on until 1927 if we so desire. As I have already said, I have not the least doubt we shall be able to command such support as we all along have had in the House of Commons at another session, but shall we be able to do more than that? That is the question 1 have put to every one of my colleagues in the government and to not a few of 116 members. It is a question I now put to you who have honoured me with your representation in the House of Commons. It is a question I put to the electorate of this country. Is it sufficient that, as a government, we should continue in office, drawing our indemnities and salaries as members and ministers, and enjoying -the other fruits of office, when great national questions press for solution, with which, -for want of an adequate majority in parliament we are unable satisfactorily to cope?
And then, after stating the difficult position of his party in the House when they had a majority, if I remember rightly, of 130 members combined, the right hon. gentleman proceeded :
I have come to the conclusion that it -is not in the national interests further to postpone the day when questions that are pressing urgently for a solution can be dealt with in a reasonable and satisfactory manner.
Then, having digressed to make a personal attack on the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), in which the country was not then nor is now particularly interested, the Prime Minister continued:
We could, I believe, so arrange our sessional programme as to continue to command in the House of Commons a support equal to that we have had during the last four years. But I doulbt if we could do more than that. I doubt if, on -the eve of a general election, we could introduce in parliament any great measure of reform without its whole aim and purpose being misconstrued and the legislation itself being thwarted. At most we would be reduced to marking time. This is not a moment in our country's affairs at which to hark time; dt is a time to march forward.
Then approaching the very heart of the problem, in which the whole country was then and is now most deeply interested, more intensely interested, I think, than in the subject matter of the present Address, and upon which the future prosperity, I might almost say, the ultimate destiny of Canada depends, the Prime Minister said:
That brings me to a consideration of three outstanding national problems o-f the greatest importance

-the transportation problem, itihe problem of immigration, and the fiscal problem. To these I should add a fourth, the constitution and powers of the Senate. I can see no solution - of the problems of taxation, no means of reducing materially our public debt, our income tax, our sales tax, and other taxes, apart from a satisfactory solution of the four problems here mentioned, all of which are inter-related and in more ways than one inseparably intertwined. May I say .further, I believe each of the problems mentioned is a pressing one. I do not believe that any one of the four can be dealt with effectually at a last session of .parliament. They can only be satisfactorily dealt with by a House of Commons (fresh from the people and with a mandate (from the people to carry out their will.
You will notice, Sir, there was no mention of rural credits, of the Hudson Bay railway or of old age pensions. He was discussing the four problems which the whole country then recognized to be vital, and upon which he was proceeding to invite the decision of the electorate and their mandate for the next four years. He proceeded:
I would say, further, I do not believe that any of the four can be dealt with effectively by a government which is not supported by a substantial majority in the House of Commons. Group government and minority government may be inevitable in transitional phases of our political history, but neither is the kind of government wherewith to achieve great reforms. In both Great Britain and the United States the electorate has shown within the very recent past that it wishes no more of either form, that what each believes the existing situation requires is a national party representative of all parts of the country, sufficiently strong in the representation it sends to parliament to insure the carrying out by the government of its plans and policies.
That is the pronouncement made by a party which went to the country, and which now stands with a greatly reduced representation in this House, assisted by the Progressive party, whose numbers have been reduced from 65 to 24-the Liberal party which now day by day in the eyes of the whole country shows that it is utterly incapable of properly carrying out the business of the Dominion-of functioning as a government. Then the Prime Minister proceeded to contend that his government was not solely responsible for the National railway system, in which contention we all agree, I think. He declared that despite the management of the National Railways, which, as he alleged, had been placed beyond political control, we must nevertheless admit that the balance sheets of the National Railways are of as much concern to the people of Canada as the balance sheets of the national ledger in all other particulars. He said:
The railway problem .to my mind is the most important of all problems pressing for immediate solution. Can taxation be substantially reduced until we have overcome the deficits on our National Railways? Can the National Railways or the Canadian Pacific Railway reduce rates so long as there are

deficits in the case of the one and a reduction in earnings in the case of the other?
Then he added:
There are many measures that might be adopted under the authority of parliament which would be to the advantage alike of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and of benefit also to the general public. It is not for me at this time to say in any final way what those measures should be.
Finality in this, as in all matters of legislative enactment, belong to parliament.
Referring to the appointment by the government of Sir Henry Thornton as executive head of the Canadian National Railway system, he continued:
It must be apparent, however, that something more is needed if government ownership os to have a fair trial in the fullest meaning of the words. So long as the system is handicapped by deficits, due in the main to encumbrances of the .past for which the present management and directorate are in no way responsible, it cannot be said that government ownership is having a fair trial. It is equally true that so long as deficits on the National Railways continue, freight rates cannot be appreciably reduced, nor can our national taxation.
Then he referred to the competition for freight and passenger traffic which now exists between the two great railway systems, and added:
The situation is aggravated by the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway is the largest single taxpayer into the federal treasury. Is that a position that is easily defensible, or defensible for long?
Proceeding with his discussion of the possibility of developing a policy of "regulated and controlled competition," the Prime Minister said:
What I want to make clear and repeat at the moment	is	that we	have	no	problem	more urgentlyin need	of	solution	than	the	railway	problem, thatwithout	its	solution	there	is	little or	no chance ofreducing	our national	debt	and the income and other
taxes, to say nothing of railway rates; that in the interests alike of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the public its solution must not be delayed, and that the solution can be worked out and given effect to only by a government that has a strong support in parliament and a mandate from the people to act. I am prepared to say that if given such a majority the present government will take up its task immediately and at an early date present to parliament the necessary legislation.
The hon. gentleman insists that he received his mandate from the people, but I notice in the Speech from the Throne there is an entire absence of any suggestion that the necessary legislation to effect these reforms will be introduced by the government during the present session.
